s: Alhucemas is situated at Wad Nechor (at the river mouth)
q: Alhucemos, is another small island and _praesidio_ of the Spaniards, containing five or six hundred inhabitants; it commands the bay of the same name, and is situate at the mouth of the river Wad Nechor, where there is also the Islet of Ed-Housh.

s: Penon de Velez is a Spanish presidio-island (convict settlement)
q: Penon de Velez is the third _praesidio_-island, a convict settlement of the Spaniards on this coast, and a very strong position, situate opposite the mouths of the river Gomera, which disembogues in the Mediterranean.

s: Penon de Velez has population nine hundred inhabitants (garrison population)
q: The garrison contains some nine hundred inhabitants.

s: Penon de Velez is supplied with fresh water (part of the year from the mainland)
q: So far as natural resources are concerned, Penon de Velez is a mere rock, and a part of the year is obliged to be supplied with fresh water from the mainland.

s: Gomera is a city (opposite Penon de Velez; ancient Parientina or possibly Acra of Ptolemy)
q: Immediately opposite to the continent is the city of Gomera (or Badis), the ancient Parientina, or perhaps the Acra of Ptolemy, afterwards called Belis, and by the Spaniards, Velez de la Gomera.

s: Gomera is named after Gomeres (according to J.A. Conde)
q: The name Gomera, according to J.A. Conde, is derived from the celebrated Arab tribe of the Gomeres, who flourished in Africa and Spain until the last Moorish kings of Granada.

s: Rif is rich in mines
q: The Rif country is full of mines, and is bounded south by one of the lesser chains of the Atlas running parallel with the coast.

s: Morocco is divided into Central Region (natural regional division)
q: II. The Central Region, or the great chain of the Atlas.

s: Rif is inhabited by Berbers (warlike and semi-barbarous population)
q: The provinces of Rif and Garet, containing these maritime towns are rich and highly cultivated, but inhabited by a warlike and semi-barbarous race of Berbers, over whom the Emperor exercises an extremely precarious authority.

s: Rif is a refuge for Abd-el-Kader (after his retirement from Algeria)
q: Among these tribes, Abd-el-Kader sought refuge and support when he was obliged to retire from Algeria, and, where he defied all the power of the Imperial government for several months.

s: Tetouan is a large mercantile city (in the province of Hasbat; four or five miles from the sea)
q: Tetuan, the Yagath of the Romans, situate at the opening of the Straits of Gibraltar, four or five miles from the sea, upon the declivity of a hill and within two small ranges of mountains, is a fine, large, rich and mercantile city of the province of Hasbat.

s: Tetouan has port Marteen (nearby port on Wad Marteen)
q: on its banks is the little port of Marteen or Marteel, not quite two miles distant from the coast, and about three from the city, where a good deal of commerce is carried on

s: Tetouan has population nine to twelve thousand souls (including Moors, Arabs, Jews and Berbers)
q: The population of Tetouan is from nine to twelve thousand souls, including, besides Moors and Arabs, four thousand Jews, two thousand <DW64>s, and eight thousand Berbers.

s: Tetouan has suburbs gardens and plantations (olive, vine and orange cultivation)
q: The suburbs are adorned with fine gardens, and olive and vine plantations. Orange groves, or rather orange forests, extend for miles around, yielding their golden treasures.

s: Tetouan is situated southeast of Tangier (about two-thirds of a day's journey)
q: The town is about two-thirds of a day's journey from Tangier, south-east.

s: Ceuta is a ancient city and fortress (formerly capital of Mauritania Tingitana)
q: Ceuta is considered to be Esilissa of Ptolemy, and was once the capital of Mauritania Tingitana.

s: Ceuta is situated near Gibraltar (fourteen miles south and nearly opposite)
q: It is a very ancient city and celebrated fortress, situate fourteen miles south of Gibraltar, nearly opposite to it, as a species of rival stronghold

s: Ceuta occupies peninsula (detaching from the continent on the east and turning north)
q: It is a very ancient city and celebrated fortress, situate fourteen miles south of Gibraltar, nearly opposite to it, as a species of rival stronghold, and placed upon a peninsula, which detaches itself from the continent on the east, and turns then to the north.

s: Morocco is divided into Southern Atlas region (quasi-Saharan natural region)
q: III. South of the Atlas: or quasi-Saharan region, comprising the various provinces and districts of Sous, Sidi Hisham, Wadnoun, Guezoula, Draha (Draa), Tafilett, and a large portion of the Sahara, south-east of the Atlas.

s: Ceuta includes Monte-del-Acho (citadel location)
q: the citadel occupies Monte-del-Acho, called formerly Jibel-el-Mina, a name still preserved in Almina, a suburb to the south-east.

s: Ceuta was conquered by Portuguese (first Portuguese occupation in Africa)
q: On 21st of August, 1415, the Portuguese conquered it, and it was the first place which they occupied in Africa.

s: Ceuta was transferred to Spain's North African presidios (after Portugal passed into Spanish power)
q: In 1578, at the death of Don Sebastian, Ceuta passed with Portugal and the rest of the colonies into the power of Spain; and when, in 1640, the Portuguese recovered their independence, the Spaniards were left masters of Ceuta, which continues still in their hands, but is of no utility to them except as a _praesidio_, which makes the fourth penal settlement possessed by them on this coast.

s: Ceuta is a Spanish presidio (fourth penal settlement on the coast)
q: the Spaniards were left masters of Ceuta, which continues still in their hands, but is of no utility to them except as a _praesidio_, which makes the fourth penal settlement possessed by them on this coast.

s: Ceuta has garrison two or three thousand men
q: Ceuta contains a garrison of two or three thousand men.

s: Ceuta has free population five or six thousand
q: The free population amounts to some five or six thousand.

s: Ceuta has port small and insecure port
q: It has a small and insecure port.

s: Ceuta has landmark Gibel Zaterit (also called Monkey's promontory or Ape's Hill)
q: Here is the famed Gibel Zaterit, "Monkey's promontory," or "Ape's Hill,"

s: Gibraltar is a European pillar of Hercules (opposite the African pillar)
q: Anciently, the mountains hereabouts formed the African pillars of Hercules opposite to Gibraltar, which may be considered the European pillar of that respectable hero of antiquity.

s: Fez is a kingdom (historically)
q: Fez itself formed a powerful kingdom, extending itself eastward as far as the gates of Tlemsen.

s: Fez is separated from Morocco (by the river Bouragrag)
q: The ancient division mentioned by Leo was that of two large provinces of Morocco and Fez, separated by the river Bouragrag, which empties itself into the sea between Rabat and Salee; and, indeed, for several centuries, these districts were separated and governed by independent princes.

s: Arzila is a ancient Berber city
q: Arzila or Asila, in the province of Hasbat, which is an ancient Berber city

s: El Araish is a town town (on the Atlantic)
q: The next town on the Atlantic, after another day's journey southwards, is El Araish

s: El Araish is in Azgar (as district capital)
q: the greater part of the district of Azgar, of which it is the capital and the residence of the Governor.

s: El Araish replaces Lixus (ancient city)
q: This city replaces the ancient Liscas or Lixus and Lixa, whose ruins are near.

s: El Araish is named vine trellices (meaning of the name)
q: The next town on the Atlantic, after another day's journey southwards, is El Araish, _i.e._, the trellices of vines

s: El Araish has population 4,000 souls (2,700 Moors and 1,300 Jews according to one account)
q: El-Araish contains a population of 2,700 Moors, and 1,300 Jews, or 4,000 souls

s: El Araish has garrison 500 troops
q: It has a garrison of 500 troops.

s: El Araish is situated on Cos River (at the river mouth and on a small promontory)
q: The town is situate upon a small promontory stretching into the sea, and along the mouth of the river Cos, or Luccos (Loukkos)

s: El Araish has port secure port (formed by the Cos or Luccos River, but difficult to enter)
q: which forms a secure port, but of so difficult access, that vessels of two hundred tons can scarcely enter it.

s: El Araish has fortifications good (made by the Spaniards)
q: the fortifications are good, because made by the Spaniards

s: El Araish was captured by Spanish (in 1610)
q: the Spaniards, who captured this place in 1610

s: Arzila is in Hasbat
q: Arzila or Asila, in the province of Hasbat

s: El Araish was recaptured by Muley Ishmael (in 1689)
q: but it was re-taken by Muley Ishmael in 1689.

s: El Araish produces cotton (in the environs)
q: In the environs, cotton is cultivated

s: El Araish exports cork
q: El-Araish exports cork, wool, skins, bark, beans, and grain

s: Azgar is a district (with El Araish as capital)
q: the district of Azgar, of which it is the capital and the residence of the Governor.

s: Azgar is inhabited by Beni-Arous (the Beni-Arous populate most of the district)
q: a powerful tribe, who populate the greater part of the district of Azgar

s: Lixus is a ancient city (replaced by El Araish)
q: This city replaces the ancient Liscas or Lixus and Lixa, whose ruins are near.

s: Lixus has coins Lixus coins (five classes remain)
q: The ancient Lixus deserves farther mention on account of the interest attached to its coins, a few of which remain, although but very recently deciphered by archeologists. There are five classes of them

s: Lixus coins are made by Phoenicians (all five classes)
q: and all Phoenician

s: Mauritania is rich and fertile (excepting a small desert part)
q: Mauritania generally, excepting a small part desert, is rich and fertile, well watered with rivers and washed with lakes; abounding in all things

s: Arzila is named Zilia (under Roman rule)
q: which, when conquered by the Romans, was named first Zilia

s: Mehedia is also called Mamora (sometimes, Nuova Mamora)
q: Mehedia or Mamora, and sometimes, Nuova Mamora, is situate upon the north-western <DW72> of a great hill

s: Mehedia is situated on Sebon River (on its left bank at the mouth)
q: upon the left bank of the mouth of the Sebon

s: Mehedia is in Beni-Hassan (province)
q: at the edge of the celebrated plain and forest of Mamora, belonging to the province of Beni-Hassan.

s: Mehedia was built by Jakob-el-Mansour (to defend the river mouth)
q: According to Marmol, Mamora was built by Jakob-el-Mansour to defend the embouchure of the river.

s: Mehedia was captured by Spanish (in 1614)
q: It was captured by the Spaniards in 1614

s: Mehedia was recaptured by Moors (in 1681)
q: and retaken by the Moors in 1681.

s: Salee is a ancient city (near the mouth of the Bouragrag River)
q: Salee or Sala, a name which this place bore antecedently to the Roman occupation, is a very ancient city

s: Salee is situated on Bouragrag River (on the right bank near its mouth)
q: situate upon the right bank of the river Bouragrag, and near its mouth.

s: Salee is in Beni-Hassan (province)
q: The modern Salee is a large commercial and well-fortified city of the province of Beni-Hassan.

s: Arzila is named Zulia (subsequently under Roman rule)
q: and afterwards Zulia, _Constantia Zilis_.

s: Salee has population two or three thousand (according to a resident; higher estimates are considered exaggerated)
q: A resident of this country reduces the population of Salee as low as two or three thousand.

s: Salee rovers use Salee (as a former rendezvous)
q: For many years, the port of Salee was the rendezvous of the notorious pirates of Morocco

s: Salee rovers is ferocious and courageous the most ferocious and courageous in the world
q: these Salee rovers were at once the most ferocious and courageous in the world.

s: Salee rovers operate near Lundy Island (formerly intercepting British traders)
q: Time was, when these audacious freebooters lay under Lundy Island in the British Channel, waiting to intercept British traders!

s: Bouragrag River separates Salee (from Rabat)
q: is situated on the declivity of a hill, opposite to Salee, on the other side of the river

s: Rabat is a modern city (large, densely populated, strong and well-built)
q: Rabat, or Er-Rabat, and on some of the foreign maps Nuova Sale, is a modern city of considerable extent, densely populated, strong and well-built

s: Rabat is in Temsna (province)
q: belonging to the province of Temsna.

s: Rabat is situated opposite Salee (across the Bouragrag River)
q: situated on the declivity of a hill, opposite to Salee, on the other side of the river

s: Rabat was built by Jakob-el-Mansour (and named Rabat-el-Fatah)
q: It was built by the famous Yakob-el-Mansour, nephew of Abd-el-Moumen, and named by him Rabat-el-Fatah

s: Arzila is on Atlantic Ocean (on the naked shore)
q: It is placed on the naked shores of the Atlantic, and has a little port.

s: Rabat has walls large enclosed space
q: The walls of Rabat enclose a large space of ground

s: Rabat has population three or four thousand Jews (some wealthy and influential)
q: Among the population are three or four thousand Jews, some of them of great wealth and consequence.

s: Rabat trades with Fez (and other interior places)
q: The merchants are active and intelligent, carrying on commerce with Fez, and other places of the interior

s: Rabat trades with Genoa (foreign commerce)
q: as also with the foreign ports of Genoa, Gibraltar, and Marseilles.

s: Rabat trades with Gibraltar (foreign commerce)
q: as also with the foreign ports of Genoa, Gibraltar, and Marseilles.

s: Rabat trades with Marseilles (foreign commerce)
q: as also with the foreign ports of Genoa, Gibraltar, and Marseilles.

s: Rabat is inhabited by Moors (mostly expelled from Spain)
q: The Moors of Rabat are mostly from Spain, expelled thence by the Spaniards.

s: Jakoub Almanzor intends Rabat (as his capital)
q: The famous Sultan, Almanzor, intended that Rabat should be his capital.

s: Jakoub Almanzor has mausoleum at Rabat (untenanted and in a separate sacred quarter)
q: His untenanted mausoleum is placed here, in a separate and sacred quarter.

s: Jakoub Almanzor expels Moravedi (from Spain)
q: This prince, surnamed "the victorious," (Elmansor,) was he who expelled the Moravedi from Spain.

s: Arzila has population about one thousand
q: The population is about one thousand.

s: Dar-el-Beida is a small town (formerly Portuguese-held)
q: Dar-el-Beida (or Casa-Blanco, "white house,") is a small town, formerly in possession of the Portuguese

s: Dar-el-Beida was built on Anfa (Portuguese construction on its ruins)
q: who built it upon the ruins of Anfa or Anafa

s: Dar-el-Beida is in Shawiya (on the borders of its fertile plains)
q: Dar-el-Beida is situate on the borders of the fertile plains of the province of Shawiya

s: Dar-el-Beida has population about one thousand inhabitants (some estimates reduce it to two hundred)
q: but now it scarcely contains above a thousand inhabitants, and some reduce them to two hundred.

s: Azamor is a ancient city (in the province of Dukaila)
q: Azamor, or Azemmour, which is an ancient and fine city of the province of Dukaila

s: Azamor is in Dukaila (province)
q: an ancient and fine city of the province of Dukaila

s: Azamor is situated on Omm-er-Rbia River (on its southern bank, near its mouth)
q: not far from the mouth of the Wad-Omm-er-Rbia (or Omm-Erbegh) on its southern bank

s: Azamor produces Shebbel salmon (principal commerce and source of profit)
q: The Shebbel salmon is the principal commerce, and a source of immense profit to the town.

s: Azamor was captured by Portuguese (in 1513)
q: Azamor was taken by the Portuguese under the command of the Duke of Braganza in 1513

s: Azamor was abandoned by Portuguese (about a century after its capture)
q: but it was abandoned a century afterwards

s: Mazagran is a ancient and strong castle (on a peninsula at the bottom of a bay)
q: Mazagran, _i. e_. the above Amayeeghs, an extremely ancient and strong castle, erected on a peninsula at the bottom of a spacious and excellent bay.

s: Mazagran is named Castillo Real (Portuguese name)
q: It was rebuilt by the Portuguese in 1506, who gave it the name of Castillo Real.

s: Mazagran is named El-Bureeja (Arabic name meaning the citadel)
q: The Arabs, however, call it El-Bureeja, i.e., "the citadel."

s: Mazagran was abandoned by Portuguese (in 1769; their last stronghold in Morocco)
q: The Portuguese abandoned it in 1769; Mazagran was the last stronghold which they possessed in Morocco.

s: Mazagran has population two or three hundred
q: Its population is two or three hundred.

s: Saffee is a ancient city (in the province of Abda)
q: Saffee, or properly Asafee, called by the natives Asfee, and anciently Soffia or Saffia, is a city of great antiquity, belonging to the province of Abda

s: Saffee is in Abda (province)
q: a city of great antiquity, belonging to the province of Abda

s: Portuguese possess Arzila (formerly)
q: Whilst possessed by the Portuguese, it was a place of considerable strength

s: Saffee was built by Carthaginians (near Cape Pantin)
q: and was built by the Carthaginians near Cape Pantin.

s: Saffee has population about one thousand (including miserable Jews)
q: The population amounts to about one thousand, including a number of miserable Jews.

s: Saffee has walls massive and high
q: The walls of Saffee are massy and high.

s: Saffee was captured by Portuguese (in 1508)
q: The Portuguese captured this city in 1508

s: Saffee was abandoned by Portuguese (in 1641)
q: voluntarily abandoning it in 1641.

s: Saffee salt lake is near Saffee (about forty miles southeast)
q: About forty miles distant, S.E., is a large salt lake.

s: Moors neglect Arzila fortifications (as usual)
q: but its fortifications being, as usual, neglected by the Moors, are now rapidly decaying.

s: Imperial Cities of Morocco is a royal capitals (of the interior)
q: The royal or capitals of the interior now demand our attention, which are El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco.

s: Battle of the Three Kings causes deaths of Muley Moluc (died during the battle but not in the fighting)
q: But one of them, Muley Moluc, died very ill in a litter, and was not killed in the fight; his death, however, was kept a secret till the close of the battle

s: Battle of the Three Kings causes deaths of Portuguese nobility and chivalry (including the flower of the nobility and chivalry)
q: With their prince, Don Sebastian, perished the flower of the Portuguese nobility and chivalry of that time.

s: Mequinez is a royal residence (and city of the province of Fez)
q: Mequinez, [25] in Arabic, Miknas (or Miknasa), is a royal residence, and city of the province of Fez

s: Mequinez is in province of Fez (situated upon a hill)
q: Mequinez, [25] in Arabic, Miknas (or Miknasa), is a royal residence, and city of the province of Fez, situate upon a hill in the midst of a well-watered and most pleasant town

s: Mequinez was founded by Meknasab (a Berber tribe and fraction of the Zenatah)
q: It was founded by the tribe of Berbers Meknasab, a fraction of the Zenatah, in the middle of the tenth century

s: Mequinez has population twenty thousand souls (some estimates give forty or fifty thousand)
q: The population amounts to about twenty thousand souls, (some say forty or fifty thousand)

s: Mequinez contains Imperial guard (about nine thousand troops)
q: in which are included about nine thousand <DW64> troops, constituting the greater portion of the Imperial guard.

s: El-Kesar is a fortified place (in the province of the Gharb)
q: El-Kesar is in the province of the Gharb, and situate on the southern bank of the Luccos; here is a deep and rapid stream, flowing W. 1/4 N.W. The town is nearly as large as Tetuan, but the streets are dirty and narrow, and many of the houses in a ruinous condition, This fortified place was once adorned by some fifteen mosques, but only two or three are now fit for service.

s: Mequinez contains Spanish hospitium at Mequinez (for ransom and recovery of Christian slaves)
q: During the times of piracy, there was here, as also at Morocco, a Spanish hospitium for the ransom and recovery of Christian slaves.

s: Fez is a city (second city of Islamism and capital of the western Muslim world)
q: From that period, however, Fez [26] dates its modern celebrity and rank among the Mahometan capitals of the world, and especially as being the second city of Islamism, and the "palace of the Mussulmen Princes of the West."

s: Fez contains El-Karoubin (famous mosque supported by three hundred pillars)
q: The most famous of these temples of worship is El-Karoubin (or El-Karouiin), supported by three hundred pillars.

s: El-Karoubin contains library of antiquity at El-Karoubin (the existence of its ancient contents is presented as conjectural)
q: In this is preserved the celebrated library of antiquity, where, it is pretended, ancient Greek and Latin authors are to be found in abundance with the lost books of Titus Livy. This appears to be mere conjecture.

s: Fez contains University of Fez (formerly celebrated)
q: The university of Fez was formally much celebrated, but little of its learning now remains.

s: Fez contains Al-Kaisseriah (great commercial square)
q: In the great square, called Al-Kaisseriah, is exhibited all the commerce of Europe and Africa--nay, even of the whole world.

s: Fez has caravans to Timbuctoo (annual caravan to Central Africa)
q: Fez has two annual caravans; one leaves for Central Africa, or Timbuctoo

s: Fez has caravan to Mecca (annual caravan of pilgrims)
q: Fez has two annual caravans; one leaves for Central Africa, or Timbuctoo; and another for Mecca, or the caravan of pilgrims.

s: Fez has population fifty thousand (probable present population; earlier estimates were higher)
q: and the probability is, the present population of Fez does not by any means, exceed 50,000, if it reaches that number.

s: El-Kesar owes its enlargement to Sultan Almansor (who improved and beautified it)
q: El-Kesar, or Al-Kesar, [24] styled also El-Kesue-Kesar, is so named and distinguished because it owes its enlargement to the famous Sultan of Fez, Almansor, who improved and beautified it about the year 1180

s: Fez manufactures woollen haiks, silk handkerchiefs, slippers and shoes, and red felt caps (the red caps are commonly called the fez)
q: The manufactures are principally woollen haiks, silk handkerchiefs, slippers and shoes of excellent leather, and red caps of felt, commonly called the fez

s: Tafilett is a group of towns or villages (on the south-eastern side of the Atlas; inhabited partly by the Imperial family)
q: Tafilett consists of a group of towns or villages, situate on the south-eastern side of the Atlas, which may he added to the royal cities, being inhabited in part by the Imperial family

s: Tafilett is the birthplace of Shereefs (country of the Shereefs)
q: and is the birth-place of their sovereign power--emphatically called Beladesh-Sherfa, "country of the Shereefs."

s: Tafilett was anciently called Sedjelmasa (name retained until 1530)
q: The country was anciently called Sedjelmasa, and retained this name up to 1530 A.D., when the principal city acquired the apellation of Tafilett

s: Tafilett is inhabited by Shereefs (a castle-town is inhabited entirely by the Prophet’s family)
q: There is also a castle, or rather small town, upon the left side of the river, called by the ordinary name of Kesar, which is in the hands of the Shereefs, and inhabited entirely by the family of the Prophet.

s: Tafilett is called Ghourlan (residence of the Governor of the province of Ressant)
q: The principal and most flourishing place was a long time called Tafilett, but is now according to Callie, Ghourlan, and the residence of the Governor of the province of Ressant

s: Tafilett has population ten thousand (estimate entirely conjectural)
q: The present population has been estimated at some ten thousand, but this is entirely conjectural.

s: Tafilett is a great mart of traffic (and rendezvous of caravans through the Sahara)
q: Besides being a rendezvous of caravans, radiating through all parts of the Sahara, Tafilett is a great mart of traffic in the natural products of the surrounding countries.

s: Morocco was built by Yousel-Ben-Tashfin (King of Samtuna and founder of the Almoravedi dynasty’s capital)
q: Morocco was built in 1072 or 1073 by the famous Yousel-Ben-Tashfin, King of Samtuna, and of the dynasty of the Almoravedi, or Marabouts.

s: Morocco is situated at foot of Atlas Mountains (on the plain of Rhamma)
q: This vast city lies at the foot of the Atlas, or about fourteen miles distant, spread over a wide and most lovely plain of the province of Rhamma

s: El-Kesar is situated on Luccos (southern bank)
q: El-Kesar is in the province of the Gharb, and situate on the southern bank of the Luccos; here is a deep and rapid stream, flowing W. 1/4 N.W.

s: Morocco is watered by Tensift (the river flows six miles from the city gates)
q: spread over a wide and most lovely plain of the province of Rhamma, watered by the river Tensift, six miles from the gates of the capital.

s: Morocco has population forty to fifty thousand inhabitants (including 4,000 Shelouhs and 5,000 Jews; estimates vary)
q: but, at the present time, there are only some forty to fifty thousand inhabitants, including 4,000 Shelouhs and 5,000 Jews.

s: Morocco contains El-Kirtubeeah (principal mosque with an extremely lofty minaret)
q: The mosques are numerous and rich, the principal of which are El-Kirtubeeah, of elegant architecture with an extremely lofty minaret

s: Morocco contains El-Maazin (principal mosque; three hundred years old)
q: El-Maazin, which is three hundred years old, and a magnificent building

s: Morocco contains Benious (principal mosque; nearly seven hundred years old)
q: and Benious, built nearly seven hundred years ago of singular construction, uniting modern and ancient architecture.

s: Morocco contains Sidi Belabbess (mosque of the patron saint)
q: The mosque of the patron saint is Sidi Belabbess.

s: Morocco has caravans to Wadnoun (trade caravans pass through it to the south)
q: this capital has also its caravans, which trade to the interior, passing through Wadnoun to the south.

s: Morocco is residence of Sultan of Morocco (for one third of his time)
q: The Emperor usually resides for a third portion of his time at Morocco the rest at Fez and Mequinez.

s: Shereefian dynasty belongs to Morocco (not to Fez; a southern Shereef dynasty)
q: The present dynasty belongs not to Fez, but to Morocco; though a dynasty of Shereefs, they are Shereefs of the south, and African blood flows in their veins.

s: Shereefian dynasty is a dynasty of Shereefs (southern and African in origin)
q: The present dynasty belongs not to Fez, but to Morocco; though a dynasty of Shereefs, they are Shereefs of the south, and African blood flows in their veins.

s: El-Kesar is in Gharb
q: El-Kesar is in the province of the Gharb

s: Sultan of Morocco resides in Fez (generally prefers Fez to maintain northern allegiance)
q: The Sultan generally is obliged to give a preference to Fez for a residence, because his presence is necessary to maintain the allegiance of the north country

s: Sultan of Morocco resides in Mequinez (part of his usual residence pattern)
q: The Emperor usually resides for a third portion of his time at Morocco the rest at Fez and Mequinez.

s: Sultan of Morocco resides in Morocco (part of his usual residence pattern)
q: The Emperor usually resides for a third portion of his time at Morocco the rest at Fez and Mequinez.

s: Shereefs inhabit Tafilett (the district is their country of origin and includes the Prophet’s family)
q: Tafilett consists of a group of towns or villages, situate on the south-eastern side of the Atlas, which may he added to the royal cities, being inhabited in part by the Imperial family, and is the birth-place of their sovereign power--emphatically called Beladesh-Sherfa, "country of the Shereefs."

s: France may awaken the slumbering energies of the population (of these once flourishing and august cities)
q: France may awaken the slumbering energies of the population of these once flourishing and august cities

s: Moorish civilization is in decline sere and yellow leaf (described as nearly defunct)
q: But all these royal cities are on the decline, the "sere and yellow leaf" of a well nigh defunct civilization.

s: El-Kesar has population four or five thousand souls (not exceeding this number)
q: The population does not exceed four or five thousand souls, and some think this number over-estimated.

s: El-Kesar hosts Battle of the Three Kings (site of the battle)
q: It was at El-Kesar, where, in A.D. 1578, the great battle of The Three Kings came off

s: Battle of the Three Kings is a battle (fought at El-Kesar)

s: James M. Goodhue describes the technological development and working conditions of St. Paul daily newspapers from the 1850s through the Civil War. He recounts competition among the Pioneer, Minnesotian, Times, and later the Press for state-printing contracts, political news, telegraph reports, and presidential messages. The account includes the 1857 constitutional convention, the 1858 Atlantic cable news race, the 1859 political campaign, and the newspapers’ responses to wartime events. It also describes patriotism among printers, the First Battle of Bull Run, and preparations for resistance to the United States Army draft.

l: James M. Goodhue, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: James M. Goodhue presents a retrospective account of how newspaper production and news gathering in St. Paul changed during the latter half of the nineteenth century. He recounts disputes, competitions, labor conditions, political events, and wartime experiences involving local newspapers.

l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: St. Paul had several competing daily newspapers, including the Pioneer, Minnesotian, and Times, and later the Press. Its newspapers relied on steamboats, mail coaches, and eventually telegraph lines for news from elsewhere.

l: daily newspapers, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: The early St. Paul daily newspapers operated with small staffs and old hand presses. They competed to publish political speeches, presidential messages, telegraphic reports, and other breaking news before their rivals.

l: Pioneer Press, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: The Sunday Pioneer Press is used as an example of the enormous labor that printing a large edition would have required with nineteenth-century hand presses and hand composition. The paper is also associated with the proof press purchased for the Minnesotian, which was later still in use in the Pioneer Press composing room.

The Minnesotian printed the proceedings of the Republican constitutional convention under a state-printing contract and purchased the first Hoe press brought to Minnesota. It competed aggressively for news, published an early illustrated local feature, and was deceived when the Pioneer circulated bogus telegraphic reports.

The Pioneer printed the proceedings of the Democratic constitutional convention and competed with the Minnesotian and Times for political and telegraphic news. It secretly obtained telegraph service, retained a news monopoly for a time, and later tricked the Minnesotian with fabricated dispatches.

The Times competed with the Pioneer and Minnesotian for presidential messages and telegraphic news. It copied the bogus reports from the Minnesotian, printed them, and then circulated both the false and genuine versions after learning of the deception.

Minnesota held an election in 1857 for delegates to a constitutional convention and later became a state. The state sent many men to the Civil War and eventually conducted a draft in counties that had fallen behind in their quotas.

l: constitutional convention, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: The 1857 Minnesota election chose delegates to a constitutional convention. Because the election was politically close, Republicans and Democrats held separate conventions, whose proceedings were printed by the Minnesotian and Pioneer under contract.

l: Republican Party, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: Republicans held a separate constitutional convention in 1857 and their proceedings were assigned to the Minnesotian. In 1859 they worked to elect Alexander Ramsey and their legislative ticket, bringing Galusha A. Grow and Schuyler Colfax to Minnesota as speakers.

l: Democratic Party, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: Democrats held a separate constitutional convention in 1857, and the Pioneer received the contract to print its proceedings. Minnesota Democrats later hoped that Stephen A. Douglas would be nominated for president at the Charleston convention.

l: Mr. Winslow's telegraph line, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: The completion of the Winslow telegraph line in 1860 ended a period when St. Paul newspapers depended heavily on steamboats and mail coaches for distant news. Telegraph rates were initially too high for the papers to afford easily, and the Pioneer secretly obtained service before broader arrangements were made.

l: president's message, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: The Pioneer, Minnesotian, and Times competed intensely to publish the full text of the president's message first. Printers prepared large staffs and distributed type in advance, while one Minnesotian proprietor unsuccessfully traveled to intercept an earlier copy.

l: Civil War, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: During the Civil War, many printers enlisted, making it difficult for the Press to maintain its staff. The Press supported vigorous prosecution of the war and faced threats from people hostile to the draft and to its wartime position.

l: First Battle of Bull Run, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: Initial reports of the First Battle of Bull Run announced a Union victory, causing James M. Goodhue to feel confident after attending Dan Rice's circus. Later reports revealed a major Union reverse, and Gov. Marshall expressed deep concern about the country's prospects.

l: Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: Abraham Lincoln issued a response concerning the Minnesota draft: "If the draft cannot take place, of course it cannot take place. Necessity knows no law. A. Lincoln." The statement was telegraphed after the provost marshal was not ready to conduct the draft on the designated day.

l: United States Army draft, Novel-10146, If James M.
s: A draft was ordered in several Minnesota counties whose populations had fallen behind their military quotas. Opposition was strong, troops were brought from the fort in anticipation of disorder, and the draft ultimately took place without interruption.

s: The unnamed narrator describes newspaper publishing in St. Paul before and after the Civil War, including holiday publication practices and competition among local papers. On July 4, 1863, the Pioneer was moving offices while the Press alone issued an extra reporting the Union victories at Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg, prompting a major celebration in St. Paul. The narrator began working for the Daily Minnesotian in 1858 and explains how the Pioneer scooped competing papers with news of Minnesota's admission into the Union before telegraphic communication existed. The unit also traces technological changes in newspaper production from single-cylinder presses to stereotyping and linotype machines.

s: The unit describes steamboat travel on the upper Mississippi, especially the activity of the Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company and St. Paul's levee. It recounts the Five Million Loan Election, the issuance and later compromise of Minnesota state railroad bonds, and the collapse of the associated railroad construction scheme. It also describes a 1858 battle near Shakopee between the Sioux and Chippewas and St. Paul's elaborate celebration of the successful laying of the Atlantic cable, attended by representations of Queen Victoria and James Buchanan.

l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: St. Paul was a major upper Mississippi steamboat destination, with a busy levee, numerous hotels, daily stage and steamboat connections, and a population of about 10,000 in the period described. It gave a majority of more than 4,000 for the Five Million Loan measure and held a large celebration for the successful laying of the Atlantic cable on September 1, 1858.

l: Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company operated splendid steamers serving points on the upper Mississippi. Its regular arrivals drew travelers, merchants, newspaper messengers, and town-lot dealers to St. Paul's levee.

l: Five Million Loan Election, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Five Million Loan Election concerned a constitutional amendment authorizing state aid of $10,000 per mile to four railroad companies for each mile graded and ready to iron. Leading men of both parties supported it, and the amendment passed by an immense majority after the panic of 1857.

l: Minnesotian, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Minnesotian, edited by Dr. Thomas Foster, was the only prominent paper identified as opposing the Five Million Loan measure. It later denounced Gov. Sibley and the railroad bonds as fraudulent and illegal, and its attacks caused concern that eastern investors would view them as reflecting local opinion.

l: Panic of 1857, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The panic of 1857 had a very depressing effect on business. Supporters of the Five Million Loan measure argued that it would employ thousands and revive railroad building, land speculation, and other economic activity.

l: Minnesota, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Minnesota authorized railroad aid through the Five Million Loan amendment, but the railroad companies defaulted and the state's credit was compromised when the bonds could not be negotiated. Nearly 250 miles of road were graded, and during Gov. Pillsbury's administration the state compromised with bondholders by paying 50 percent of the securities' nominal value.

l: railroad companies receiving state bonds, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Four railroad companies were to receive $10,000 in state bonds for every mile of road graded and ready to iron. They demanded that Gov. Sibley issue the bonds, rejected his restrictions, obtained a peremptory writ from the supreme court, and later defaulted when the railroad construction scheme collapsed.

l: Minnesota state bonds, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Minnesota state bonds issued for railroad construction could not be negotiated in the New York market, compromising the state's credit. They were repudiated for more than twenty years before the state compromised with their holders and paid half their nominal value.

l: Minnesota Supreme Court, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Minnesota Supreme Court issued a peremptory writ directing Gov. Sibley to issue the railroad bonds. Judge Flandrau dissented, believing the state's financial reputation would have been greatly improved had his position prevailed.

l: Henry Hastings Sibley, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Henry H. Sibley, identified in the text as Gov. Sibley, initially refused to issue the railroad bonds until the state's rights were protected. On the advice of the attorney general and in compliance with the supreme court's mandate, he reluctantly signed them and later failed to negotiate them in New York.

l: state of Minnesota, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The state of Minnesota faced a compromised credit after the railroad companies defaulted and the bonds could not be sold. It foreclosed on nearly 250 miles of graded railroad and later donated the lines to new organizations before settling with bondholders for 50 percent of the securities' nominal value.

l: Shakopee, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Shakopee was near the site of a battle in late May 1858 between Sioux and Chippewa warriors. Reporters remained in the vicinity for several days expecting further engagements.

l: Chippewas, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: A party of Chippewa warriors under Chief Hole-in-the-day surprised Sioux near Shakopee and opened fire, killing or wounding fifteen or twenty. Eight or ten Chippewas were killed during the engagement.

l: Atlantic cable, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Atlantic cable was successfully laid in 1858, allowing messages to be exchanged between Queen Victoria and President Buchanan. It operated successfully for about four weeks before the last message was exchanged on the day of St. Paul's celebration.

l: celebration of the successful laying of the Atlantic cable, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: St. Paul held an elaborate celebration on September 1, 1858, with a procession nearly two miles long, military units, floats, civic officials, secret societies, and thousands of spectators. Fireworks were postponed because of a storm, and the celebration coincided with the last message exchanged between England and America.

l: Queen Victoria, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Queen Victoria exchanged messages with President Buchanan after the Atlantic cable was completed. Her representative in St. Paul's 1858 procession was Miss Rosa Larpenteur.

l: James Buchanan, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: James Buchanan exchanged messages with Queen Victoria after the successful laying of the Atlantic cable. In St. Paul's celebration, he was represented by George Folsom, a product of the city.

l: St. Paul procession, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The St. Paul procession honoring the Atlantic cable included cavalry, bands, military companies, a city battery, civic and state officials, religious and fraternal organizations, tradespeople, floats, and citizens. It marched for three and one-half hours along a route through many city streets before reaching its destination.

l: Atlantic cable enterprise, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Atlantic cable enterprise required four attempts before success: in 1857, 1858, 1863, and 1865. The 1858 cable operated for about four weeks, while a new company laid a cable in 1866 that was in successful operation at the time described.

l: Cyrus W. Field, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Cyrus W. Field was the projector of the Atlantic cable enterprise. Congress gave him unanimous thanks, and Great Britain would have knighted him had he considered it proper to accept the honor.

l: railroad construction scheme, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The railroad construction scheme promised state bonds to companies for graded railroad mileage and was expected to revive employment and commerce after the panic of 1857. It collapsed when the bonds could not be negotiated, the companies defaulted, and the state's credit was compromised.

l: railroad development in Minnesota, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: The Five Million Loan amendment encouraged railroad development in Minnesota by offering $10,000 per mile for road graded and ready to iron. Nearly 250 miles were graded before the state foreclosed on the lines and later donated them to new organizations.

l: steamboat travel, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: Steamboat travel was described as the primary way to reach points on the upper Mississippi. During the summer it was pleasant, but winter travel east was difficult and expensive, requiring merchants to stock enough goods to last from November through April.

l: telegraphic communication, Novel-10146, THE FIVE MILLION LOAN ELECTION.
s: St. Paul had no telegraphic communication when the Atlantic cable was completed, so news of the event arrived several days late. The city later celebrated after messages had been exchanged between Queen Victoria and President Buchanan.

The order used elaborate initiations, including public confessions, frightening ceremonies, and bouncing candidates into the air; its membership and reputation declined after Rev. John Penman published an illustrated exposure of its secret work in Harper's Weekly.

s: St. Paul received a Sons of Malta lodge in 1858, and the organization quickly attracted merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and many other men. It was also the center of competing Republican and Democratic newspaper enterprises, including the Minnesotian, Times, Minnesotian and Times, St. Paul Daily Press, and Daily North Star.

s: After the 1859 election, the Republican Party secured a majority in the legislature. The Minnesotian and Times both sought the state's printing patronage, claiming equal service to the Republican ticket, and party leaders arranged their temporary consolidation to resolve the dispute.

s: The Minnesotian was a Republican paper whose editor, Dr. Foster, engaged in a bitter rivalry with Thomas M. Newson of the Times. It was temporarily consolidated with the Times as the Minnesotian and Times, then returned to Dr. Foster's control after the partnership ended. l: Times, Novel-10146, Some time during the early '50s a secret order known as the Sons of Malta was or

l: Minnesotian and Times, Novel-10146, Some time during the early '50s a secret order known as the Sons of Malta was or
s: The Minnesotian and Times was created through a politically arranged consolidation of the two rival Republican papers. l: St. Paul Press, Novel-10146, Some time during the early '50s a secret order known as the Sons of Malta was or

s: The office of state printer became the subject of a vigorous contest after the Republican victory in 1859. Moore received the printing of the journals of the two legislative houses as part of the settlement of the former newspaper partnership.

l: Sons of Malta initiation, Novel-10146, Some time during the early '50s a secret order known as the Sons of Malta was or
s: The Sons of Malta's secret initiation involved hooded candidates being questioned about their conduct before the full lodge, despite believing they were in a private chamber. The ceremony included frightening sounds, public humiliation, and other physical ordeals, including bouncing candidates from a rubber blanket. Rev. John Penman's anger over his treatment led him to publish an illustrated exposure of the secret work.

l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 began on August 18 during the Civil War, when Sioux forces attacked settlers and government personnel in western Minnesota. The attacks spread across the reservation and surrounding communities, including Fort Ridgely, New Ulm, and Birch Coulie, causing extensive deaths, destruction, and displacement. Gov. Alexander Ramsey called for emergency measures, while Henry Hastings Sibley led partially equipped forces against the Sioux. Other Day helped sixty-two refugees reach safety, and St. Paul organized home guards as fear of further attacks spread.

l: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 occurred during a critical period of the Civil War and began with an attack on August 18. It spread rapidly across western Minnesota, killing people, destroying property, and driving thousands of settlers from their homes.

l: United States government, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
s: The United States government was heavily occupied with the Civil War and was considered unprepared for the Sioux outbreak. It had delayed annuity payments, while government officers had promoted farming, supplied tools and seed, and built houses for some Sioux.
